prize_parts.citation: For the invention and development of the optical lattice clock, in which many neutral atoms trapped at a magic wavelength are interrogated at once, bringing frequency measurement to the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: After the full first-round exchange I keep B012 (Katori, Ye) as my single prize part. Seven of eight files converge on it, but what settles it for me is the argument rather than the count. The magic-wavelength lattice is a specific, original step: state-independent trapping lets thousands of neutral atoms be interrogated on a narrow transition without Doppler or recoil shifts, and that is what moved accuracy and stability together to the 10^-18 level. The result is reproduced in several laboratories, used in relativistic geodesy and in clock-based tests of fundamental constants, and its credit can be stated in two names with a citation that says what was added. This also answers the question the chair put: the overlap with the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 single-ion prize is best handled by wording the citation around many-atom lattice interrogation, not by changing the laureate list. I have not changed my preferred configuration since round 1.
statement.case_against: The credit problem has not gone away and I still cannot verify the first-demonstration history from the materials. Takamoto, Hong, Ludlow, Lemke and the NIST, PTB and SYRTE groups are outside the two names, and the strontium versus ytterbium sequence matters for fairness. I accept that a citation can only partly repair this. If the committee's own check showed that a third person had an equal claim to the lattice concept, I would reopen the two-name allocation, which is where I part from colleagues who treat the omissions as purely a wording matter. The overlap with 2005 and 2012 is a real objection, and Eriksson's preference for a conceptual discovery over an instrument is a legitimate criterion, not a bias. I also remain wary that I am comfortable with B012 partly because it lies far from my own field of string theory and cosmology; that distance is no merit of the candidate.

responses.point: Eriksson prefers B030 (Kane, Mele, Molenkamp) as the most defensible condensed-matter candidate, holds that a concept that changed how a class of materials is understood should outrank a precision-measurement advance, and treats the pending redefinition of the second as leaving the clock's impact unfinished.
responses.response: I think his criterion is fair, and the magic-wavelength lattice is arguably a concept as much as an instrument: it is a design principle about state-independent trapping, not only a better apparatus. On B030 I agree with his own caveat, which I find heavier than he does. The Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang prediction is what Molenkamp tested, Zhang is deceased, and a trio plus a citation naming the HgTe observation still reads as a partial account, on top of the 2016 prize on topological phases. I would not treat that as disqualifying, and I list B030 as an alternative, but it leaves B030 below B012 for me. On the second, I hold my round-1 view: the measurements exist and are reproduced, so the prize should not wait on a metrological decision.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks B012 first as an atomic-structure advance, state-independent trapping, that builds on but does not duplicate the combs and the single-ion work, and accepts that lattice-clock credit is wider than two names.
responses.response: Her answer is the one I find most persuasive on the overlap objection, and I asked her in round 1 how to separate neutral-atom lattice interrogation from single-ion clocks. I now propose the wording myself: the citation should name the optical lattice clock and the simultaneous interrogation of many neutral atoms at a magic wavelength, and not say accuracy in general. That keeps it apart from the comb as a tool and from ion control as a method. Her honest concession about credit beyond Katori and Ye is also what keeps me from calling the matter closed.

responses.point: Kroll argues that the comb prize recognised measurement of optical frequencies and the 2012 prize control of single quantum systems, whereas the magic-wavelength lattice is a different idea, and says the redefinition of the second is a consequence of the achievement and not a precondition.
responses.response: I agree on both points and the redefinition argument is the one I rely on. We both asked for the first-demonstration history to be checked in round 1, and I note that neither of us has been able to settle it from the files. I would push slightly further than he does: if that check cannot be done, the committee is asked to decide on a two-name allocation without having tested its main weakness, and I would want that stated openly in the discussion record, not left to the citation.

responses.point: Johansson moved to B012 but warns that ion clocks reach comparable uncertainty and that the citation should not rest on accuracy in general; he also notes that the 2005 and 2012 prizes may leave less room for another precision-measurement award.
responses.response: I agree that a citation resting on the 10^-18 number alone would invite the objection that ion clocks are equally good, so the number should follow the lattice concept in the wording and not lead it. On room for another metrology prize, I read the three prizes as honouring three different steps (measuring optical frequencies, controlling single ions, interrogating many neutral atoms), which I think is a sequence and not a repeat. He is also right in his reply to me that the Higgs attribution to founding spokespersons is more severe than the clock problem; I accepted this in round 1 and it still holds, so I do not return to B028.

responses.point: Pearce, now a B012 supporter, concedes that B042 has the larger recent scientific footprint and that the attribution there is less settled than he assumed, and he accepts that the citation should say what the lattice clock added.
responses.response: I rank B042 as the most serious competitor and he is right about its footprint. My objection is the same as before: the superconducting mechanism is unsettled, the field is under a decade old, and the credit among MacDonald, Bistritzer, Jarillo-Herrero, Cao, Dean, Young and the earlier band-flattening theorists is not settled within three names. I would be willing to look at it again in a later year if those points mature. His agreement that the citation must state the added step is what I would ask the committee to adopt.

uncertainties: Whether the first-demonstration and credit history of the strontium and ytterbium lattice clocks (Takamoto, Hong, Ludlow, Lemke, NIST, PTB, SYRTE) leaves a two-name allocation fair; I cannot verify this from the materials and it could change my view.
Whether a citation worded around many-atom magic-wavelength interrogation is enough to answer Eriksson's novelty concern, and whether he would accept B012 as lead.
Whether B042 will look more settled once the origin of its superconductivity and the experimental credit are clearer, in which case it may be the stronger candidate in a later year.
Whether a second prize part is needed at all; I do not see one that could be allocated fairly within the three-person cap.
statement.conflict_note: No change from round 1. No specific conflict is apparent from my profile: my documented connections are David Gross, Hector Rubinstein, Thomas Van Riet and the Uppsala theory group, none of whom is credited on any shortlisted ballot. My field is string theory and cosmology, and I have no research stake in atomic clocks or in the other shortlisted candidates.
